inline.s: A Textbook for Practical Practice
Living Awake: Presence, Surrender.
To practice it, there are stages of entry;
to realize it, there is the substance of one’s own attainment.
Awaken to the emptiness of all appearances, and the mind is naturally without thought.
When a thought arises, be aware at once; once aware, it is gone.
The wondrous gate of practice lies in this alone.
Be master wherever you are; wherever you stand is the real.
Perseverance is passion and persistence directed toward long-term goals.
Practice is perfected through diligence and ruined by play;
Carve without ceasing, and even metal and stone can be engraved.
The three stricts and the one large:
Strict, difficult, and starting from actual combat,
with training of large volume.
Diligently cultivate precepts, samādhi, and wisdom; extinguish greed, anger, and delusion.
[Training at the difficult level] Practice only in the “learning zone.” See
Deliberate Practice: Ten Thousand Hours to Genius
Deliberate practice:

Expert-level performance is achieved gradually through training, and the key to effective progress lies in finding a series of small tasks for the trainee to complete in sequence, so that the goal can be reached. These small tasks must be ones the trainee is just unable to do, and yet just able to learn and master. Completing such practice demands that the trainee concentrate intensely, which makes it entirely different from routine or entertainment-style practice.

Whether one is learning small life skills, such as ball games, driving, playing the piano, or cooking, or improving key work abilities, such as writing, sales, programming, or design, a great deal of practice is indispensable. But we usually hold a great misunderstanding about practice: isn’t practice just constant repetition? No! Constant repetition is merely
“naive practice”
, which brings no progress.
“Correct practice”
requires good guidance (to be self-taught is to be one’s own guide), goals, and feedback.

inline.s: Awareness Chan takes focused, continuous, and lasting awareness as its foundation for breaking through the three gates and putting an end to birth and death. This book is therefore divided into two great parts, preliminary practices and Chan contemplation: the first part is preliminary practices, the second is Chan contemplation. In the preliminary part, awareness is cultivated through the practices of awareness of movements, awareness of sensations, awareness of breathing, awareness of the present moment, and awareness of mental states. Once a firm foundation has been laid, one may then go all out in Chan contemplation.
[The three gates] Seeing one’s nature (breaking the initial gate), subduing afflictions (breaking the heavy gate), and severing afflictions (breaking the solid gate).

Note: The ancient worthies of the Chan gate spoke of three gates: first, breaking the initial gate, to understand the mind and see one’s nature (to see the nature thoroughly); second, breaking the heavy gate, to sever afflictions; third, breaking the solid gate, to realize the patient acceptance of non-arising. In light of the actual conditions of people today, Awareness Chan provisionally speaks of: first, breaking the initial gate, seeing one’s nature (glimpsing one’s own nature); second, breaking the heavy gate, subduing afflictions; third, breaking the solid gate, severing afflictions.

[Severing afflictions] Severing the delusions of views and the delusions of thought. The delusions of views are the ordinary person’s errors and confusion in views, such as the five wrong views of the view of the body, extreme views, wrong views, the view of grasping at views, and the view of attachment to precepts and observances; the delusions of thought are the ordinary person’s errors and confusion in thought, such as the afflictions of greed, anger, delusion, pride, and doubt. These two delusions are the root cause of sentient beings’ wandering through the three realms and suffering birth and death to no purpose; sever them, and one can put an end to birth and death and escape the three realms. Severing the delusions of views and thought is also called breaking the attachment to self.

[Patient acceptance of non-arising] Also called the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas: true wisdom rests securely upon the principle that “all dharmas were never born, and therefore do not cease,” and never again falls back.
Q: What is understanding the mind and seeing one’s nature?

A: Understanding the mind means stilling thoughts. Thoughts are of three kinds: coarse thoughts, subtle thoughts, and exceedingly subtle thoughts. Seeing one’s nature has two levels: glimpsing one’s own nature and seeing the nature thoroughly. When coarse and subtle thoughts are both stilled (what is ordinarily called no-thought) and one personally recognizes the thought-free essence of mind, this is glimpsing one’s own nature; for example, “pointing directly at the moment, causing one to awaken” is glimpsing one’s own nature. When exceedingly subtle thoughts are stilled as well and the nature appears thoroughly, this is seeing the nature thoroughly; for example, “the storehouse consciousness bursts open, empty space shatters” is seeing the nature thoroughly. Both kinds of seeing the nature are reached through understanding the mind (stilling thoughts), and so they are called understanding the mind and seeing one’s nature. Glimpsing one’s own nature is understanding by way of explanation (also called understanding by way of principle), whereas seeing the nature thoroughly is realization. By convention, glimpsing one’s own nature is also often called “seeing the nature,” while seeing the nature thoroughly is called “understanding the mind and seeing one’s nature.” (For the meaning and operation of one’s own nature, the nature, and the mind, see
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha

[Coarse thoughts, subtle thoughts, and exceedingly subtle thoughts] Thoughts are of three kinds: coarse thoughts, subtle thoughts, and exceedingly subtle thoughts. For a person who recites the Buddha’s name, for example, deluded thoughts are coarse thoughts and the thought of reciting the Buddha’s name is a subtle thought. Ordinarily, when coarse and subtle thoughts are both stilled, this is called no-thought—no-thought as generally understood. Further, if exceedingly subtle thoughts also come to rest, this is ultimate no-thought. Thus the meaning of the term “no-thought” must be determined from its context. [Exceedingly subtle thoughts] The exceedingly subtle arising, dwelling, and passing away of the knowing mind, which is the mark of the ālaya consciousness. When exceedingly subtle thoughts come to rest for a time, one’s own nature manifests its intrinsic state—this is understanding the mind and seeing one’s nature; when exceedingly subtle thoughts come to rest forever, one perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.

inline.s: The Avataṃsaka Sūtra
Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata says:
“There is no sentient being who does not possess the Tathāgata’s wisdom, but because of deluded thoughts, inverted views, and attachment, they do not realize it;
if they leave deluded thoughts behind
, then all-wisdom, natural wisdom, and unobstructed wisdom at once appear.”
Master Guifeng says:

“All dharmas are like a dream—so all the sages alike declare. Therefore deluded thoughts are originally still, and the dusts of sense objects are originally empty. This empty and still mind is not obscured in its spiritual knowing.
This empty and still knowing is your true nature
Whether deluded or awakened, the mind knows of itself; it does not arise through conditions, nor does it arise because of objects. The single word ‘knowing’ is the gate of all wonders.

[Empty and still knowing] Empty and still knowing is the knowing of no-knowing; to distinguish it from the knowing that grasps at appearances through seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing, it is also called “spiritual knowing.” The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says:

“To set up knowing upon seeing and knowing is the root of ignorance; when seeing and knowing are without the setting up of knowing, this is nirvāṇa, stainless and truly pure.” Master Hanshan’s Record of Contemplating the Laṅkāvatāra says: “The mind is still and yet knows; true and false are both left behind—this is named the noble wisdom of self-awakening.”
See
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha
.[The single word ‘knowing’] The word ‘knowing’ in ‘empty and still knowing.’

“Because of beginningless delusion, one falsely clings to body and mind as ‘I,’ and greed, anger, and other thoughts arise. If one meets a good friend who reveals the teaching, one may suddenly awaken to the empty and still knowing. Knowing is without thought and without form—who then is the mark of a self, who the mark of a person?

Awaken to the emptiness of all appearances, and the mind is naturally without thought. When a thought arises, be aware at once; once aware, it is gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies in this alone.

[Awaken to the emptiness of all appearances, and the mind is naturally without thought. When a thought arises, be aware at once; once aware, it is gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies in this alone] Awakening to the fact that all appearances are illusory, the mind is naturally without thought. If a deluded thought arises, one must at once awaken to the fact that one is taking the illusory as real and is being turned about by illusory appearances. Awakening to this point, the deluded thought vanishes at once. The wondrous gate of practice lies right here!
“Therefore, though one cultivates all practices fully,
one takes no-thought alone as the guiding principle

. Once the knowledge and vision of no-thought are attained, love and hate naturally grow faint, compassion and wisdom naturally increase in clarity, karmic offenses are naturally severed, and meritorious practices naturally advance. Since one understands that all appearances are not appearances, there is naturally the practice of no-practice. When afflictions are exhausted, birth and death come to an end. When arising and ceasing have ceased, stillness and illumination appear before one, functioning without end—this is called Buddha.”
(Preface to the Collected Chan Sources and Their Doctrines)

[Once the knowledge and vision of no-thought are attained] One attains the knowing and the seeing of no-thought. That is to say, one need only know without giving rise to thoughts, and see without giving rise to thoughts. This is also to mirror objects as a mirror does, without “setting up knowing upon seeing and knowing.” [Setting up knowing upon seeing and knowing] The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says:
“To set up knowing upon seeing and knowing is the root of ignorance; when seeing and knowing are without the setting up of knowing, this is nirvāṇa, stainless and truly pure.”

Thoughts are of two kinds: one is the self-directed thought, a thought one actively gives rise to, over which one has mastery, starting when one wishes and stopping when one wishes; this is called an intention, for example the thought of reciting the Buddha’s name. The other is the non-self-directed thought, over which one has no mastery and whose arising and stopping are beyond one’s control; such a thought is called a floating thought, for example “the ceaseless chatter of self-talk in the mind,” commonly known as deluded thinking.

Whether one recites the Buddha’s name or maintains a mantra, contemplates the mind or practices Chan inquiry, recites sūtras or bows to the Buddha, if one is to gain power, one must still the floating thoughts. Master Yongming says:
“Focus the mind on one place, and there is nothing that cannot be done.”
(Record of the Mirror of the School)

People either wallow in the past or calculate the future, forever spinning deluded thoughts. This is a habit deeply rooted since beginningless kalpas, like a drug addiction, and it is the source of suffering. In today’s society, with material abundance, people no longer endure the real suffering of hunger and cold; their suffering comes mainly from mental torment. Its culprit is the floating thought—the uncontrollable, endless brooding over and again. For example, a matter has long since passed, and one clearly knows that it will have no effect on the present or the future, and yet “no sooner is it off the brow than it is on the heart”: irrepressible painful memories gnaw at your heart and give rise to many physical illnesses.

The harm of floating thoughts goes far beyond mental torment and the causes of disease; more serious and more terrible still, they are the hallucinogen that clouds the spirit-consciousness and casts one into the cycle of rebirth. Everyone knows the saying, “The mad mind does not rest; when it rests, that is bodhi.” But since one already understands this principle, why will the mad mind still not rest? It is the floating thoughts that are playing tricks.

To put an end to birth and death and escape the cycle of rebirth, one must stop taking this hallucinogen—one must still the floating thoughts. When floating thoughts are stilled, one naturally becomes clear-headed, prajñā’s true wisdom appears before one, and at the moment of death one can be clear and mindful, and so leave birth and death behind. But if ordinarily one’s deluded thoughts fly about in confusion and one has no mastery over oneself, then when the many sufferings press in at the end of life, how can one keep the spirit bright and clear and not lose right mindfulness? Therefore the work of stilling floating thoughts in ordinary times is of the utmost importance.
How can one still the floating thoughts and break free from deluded thinking? The wondrous method is: awareness! Awareness is the sharp weapon that stills floating thoughts:
when aware, there is no floating thought; if a floating thought arises, it shows that awareness has been lost at that moment, and it should be taken up again at once.
When awareness becomes continuous, one naturally dwells in a state of awareness that is without thought and without thinking. The Sūtra of the Buddha’s Treasury says:
“The buddhas’ supreme perfect enlightenment is entirely without thinking and without thought.”

Since awareness and floating thoughts cannot coexist—where there is awareness there is no floating thought, and where there is a floating thought awareness has been lost—why is it that sometimes awareness and floating thoughts seem to exist at the same time? This is because awareness is neither focused nor continuous and has not yet linked up into stretches; moments of awareness and moments of floating thought alternate, and one mistakes this for the two existing side by side. Therefore, in the work of awareness, the first task is to link awareness into stretches. Once awareness forms stretches, there are naturally no floating thoughts within those stretches. In ordinary times, one should bring about as often as possible this state: aware and without floating thoughts, freed from the control of floating thoughts.

The core of the preliminary stage is this: by cultivating focused, continuous, and lasting awareness, to avoid falling into the world of the head as much as possible; and once one has fallen in, to notice it at once and step out of it. In one’s practice, one should hold to this point at all times and in all places, and the depth of one’s practice is measured by it as well.
Q: Since floating thoughts and awareness cannot coexist, then what is meant by “when a thought arises, be aware at once”?

A: The state of “when a thought arises, be aware at once” comes when the power of awareness is already very strong and one dwells in awareness at all times. Though now and then one slips and a floating thought arises (at which moment awareness is lost), one soon recovers awareness and becomes aware of the floating thought that just occurred. If the power of awareness is not strong, one often has to daydream for a while, or even for a spell, before one can become aware of it. Therefore, “when a thought arises, be aware at once” is the result of strong awareness. In study and practice, one also often uses “when a thought arises, be aware at once” to train awareness—as soon as a deluded thought arises, one must see it. At the same time, one may judge the strength of one’s awareness by how long deluded thoughts last. Master Guifeng says:
“When a thought arises, be aware at once; once aware, it is gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies in this alone.”
(Preface to the Collected Chan Sources and Their Doctrines)
Q: Why do floating thoughts arise?

A: When the manas consciousness (the mind-root) spontaneously grasps at mental objects within the ālaya consciousness and transmits them to the sixth consciousness (the mind consciousness), the thoughts that arise are floating thoughts. (For a discussion of manas, the ālaya consciousness, and the mind consciousness, see
the article on manas, the ālaya consciousness, and the mind consciousness in the study garden of our temple,
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha
, in the section “The Working Process of the Knowing Mind”

) Manas cannot do two things at once. When it is aware, it cannot grasp at mental objects; when it grasps at mental objects, awareness is certainly lost. This is the principle behind “when aware, there is no floating thought.” It is like a man who, acting as a police officer enforcing the law, will not steal; if he goes off to steal, then he is not enforcing the law. The Chan school’s phrase-observing Chan uses the observation of the phrase-head to block the mind-root
(preventing the mind-root from grasping at mental objects)
and so bring the stream of deluded thoughts to a halt. Master Hanshan says:
“Thus Great Master Dahui taught people exclusively to observe the phrase-head; his ruthless hand was only meant to make you kill the thieving mind
(the mind of feeling and knowing)

. ... All of this is the tongs and hammer that old man Dahui habitually used; his only intent was to have you block the stream of deluded thoughts beneath the mind-root with the phrase-head, and right where it is blocked, look into your original face.”
(Dream Journey Collection
Showing the Essentials of Chan Inquiry)
[Stream of deluded thoughts] The arising, dwelling, and passing away of deluded thoughts. [The stream of deluded thoughts is blocked] The stream of deluded thoughts comes to a halt.
Q: What is deluded thinking?

A: There are two kinds of thinking: self-directed thinking and non-self-directed thinking. What is generally called deluded thinking is non-self-directed thinking, in which floating thoughts follow one upon another.

The process by which the knowing mind ranges over and ponders the dusts of sense objects is: sensation → conception → action → consciousness. “Sensation” is the receiving and taking in when the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) come into contact with the six dusts (forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangible objects, and mental objects). “Conception” is the thinking (analysis, judgment, and synthesis) that arises in dependence on “sensation,” and the basis for its analysis and judgment is the mental objects drawn out from the eighth consciousness (the ālaya consciousness) by the seventh consciousness (manas). “Action” is the mental action that arises in dependence on “thinking” (the mind’s own fashioning, such as love and hate, likes and dislikes, and taking and rejecting), as well as the issuing of commands for action to body and speech—this is the creation of karma. “Consciousness” gathers all the information of the three preceding links, sensation, conception, and action, into a comprehensive discerning mark—the karmic consciousness—which is carried through the seventh consciousness into the eighth consciousness and stored there for later use. This is what is called a karmic seed, also called a mental object, and it is what manas grasps at.

[Karmic seeds] The karma created by sentient beings is stored in the ālaya consciousness; because it can produce manifest activity and so flower and bear fruit, it is called a seed. Karmic seeds are also called karmic habitual tendencies, or simply seeds and habitual tendencies. They exercise a latent influence, even a controlling one, over people’s thoughts and behavior.

In deluded thinking, however, the mind-root (manas) grasps at mental objects (karmic seeds) within the ālaya consciousness, giving rise to “sensation,” and so this cycle of the knowing mind, “sensation → conception → action → consciousness,” begins. Unbeknownst to the person, manas ceaselessly passes them along and out, and so floating thoughts follow one upon another—this is deluded thinking. For ordinary people, deluded thinking is extremely common; one may even daydream while working. When deluded thinking becomes severe, obsessive thinking appears. That is to say, one cannot stop the deluded thinking even if one wants to, and this is extremely painful.
Q: Then how does one still deluded thinking?

A: Deluded thinking can continue because the mind-root (manas) ceaselessly grasps at mental objects (karmic seeds) within the ālaya consciousness and passes them to the mind consciousness (the sixth consciousness) to think about. So long as the mind-root (manas) no longer grasps at mental objects within the ālaya consciousness, then, with no fuel supplied, the fire of deluded thinking dies out. Besides grasping at mental objects, manas has another function: awareness. And manas can perform only one function at a time: when it is aware, it cannot grasp at mental objects; when it is grasping at mental objects, awareness is lost. This is the “floating thoughts and awareness cannot coexist” spoken of above. Therefore the method for stilling deluded thinking, as stated above, is: awareness. You can verify this principle for yourself: at the very moment when you are aware in a focused and continuous way, there is no deluded thinking. The essential point of practice is to make awareness focused, continuous, and lasting. As it is said: If the seventh consciousness does not die, how can the dharma-body live? (If manas continues ceaselessly to grasp at mental objects, how can one realize the dharma-body?) The Treatise on the Universal Ground of All Being says:
“Because
(owing to)

they do not comprehend the singular dharma realm, the mind is not in accord, and suddenly a thought arises, which is named ignorance. This ignorance is also called the seventh consciousness, also called manas; it specializes in calculating and clinging to self, and is the master of discrimination and the root of ignorance. Coming and going between the sixth and the eighth
(coming and going between the sixth and eighth consciousnesses)
it passes along and out, obstructing the great bright light and veiling the original.”
[Coming and going between the sixth and the eighth] See
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha
. [The singular dharma realm] The one and only dharma realm, that is, the true mark of all dharmas. On the true mark of all dharmas (see
The True Mark of All Dharmas

Awareness Chan takes focused, continuous, and lasting awareness as its foundation in order to reach the state where the myriad thoughts return to one, the one returns to nothing, until the three gates are broken through. Therefore, in the preliminary practices, one cultivates awareness through the practices of “awareness of movements,” “awareness of sensations,” “awareness of breathing,” “awareness of the present moment,” and “awareness of mental states.” With focused, continuous, and lasting awareness as a firm foundation, one’s Chan contemplation gains power; therefore one must first of all make the foundation solid!

To make the foundation solid, one must expend great effort and undergo bitter training. Training in the basics may sometimes feel monotonous and dry, but in truth this is the best of times for refining the mind and cultivating samādhi; moreover, once the practice deepens, bitterness ends and sweetness comes, and there is a delight all its own. On this point, Mr. Li Fengshan writes in his Secret Manual of Practice:

In doing anything, one must always begin from the foundation. This is all the more so in training a skill: one must begin training from the basic work. The horse stance and the stake stance are a practice I can never forget—painful, and yet greatly beneficial. At that time, the master required us to practice the “one-character stake” well (see the figure below). For Chinese martial arts must put effort into the stake stance. In ordinary practice of boxing, one emphasizes continuity, and the speed is rather fast; but in training the stake stance, one must set the angles and adjust the posture, training endurance and power. To hold the stake stance for a considerable time depends not on physical strength but on the power of samādhi. At the age of fourteen or fifteen, to speak of the power of samādhi was truly a little difficult. But every time the master watched over our practice he would say, “Sink a little lower, sink a little lower,” strictly adjusting our movements. Sometimes, after squatting for a long time and growing tired, one would feel a stifled anger rise, and even give way to rage; once hatred arose in the mind, it became all the more impossible to squat any longer. Only later did I discover that if I still harbored anger, the mind became narrow, and there was no way to keep practicing. I told myself that I must trust the master: if he required this, there must be a reason for it; whatever the master said, that I would do. Once my attitude turned around, strangely enough, I felt steady within. I could naturally squat lower and longer. I also discovered that formerly, when I practiced the horse stance, my posture was too tense at the beginning, so that I breathed in great gasps and sometimes even held my breath; now, with the mind settled, not only could I squat longer, but my breathing was smooth. From this I also came to understand how great the mind’s function is. The mind can elevate a person or degrade him; it can save others or harm them. Those who are forever forgiving themselves, who are too narrow, or who hold no expectations of themselves, can never squat long; only by focusing the mind single-mindedly, without other thoughts, and bringing the mind to a state of non-doing, can one be calm and composed.
The plum blossom’s fragrance comes from the bitter cold

There are many objects of awareness, such as movements, sensations, breathing, scenes, the body, and mental states, and so on. All of them can be used to cultivate awareness and cut off deluded thinking. But among them, awareness of movements is the easiest—it is enough simply not to forget. Therefore, at the very beginning of the preliminary practices, one uses awareness of movements to cultivate awareness.

Awareness of movements means clearly knowing the movements as they are performed and the sensations the movements give rise to. When walking, for example, one is aware of the movement of the feet and of the sensation when the soles touch the ground; when washing one’s face, one is aware of the movements of the hands, the temperature of the water, and the sensation when the towel touches the face, and so on. Of course, one may also be aware only of the movement itself. The essential point of awareness is: focus the mind on one place, and deluded thoughts do not arise. So whatever way you find best enables you to meet this requirement, do it that way. While aware, one may silently repeat “aware” in the mind to help keep the attention fixed on awareness.

One must be focused when aware of movements; whatever one does, one should do it single-mindedly, without deluded thinking. When dressing or eating, for example, if one is aware of the movements and free of deluded thoughts, that is the state of awakening; if one daydreams while doing them, that is the state of delusion (ignorance)—the same thing is done, but “the use of the mind is different,” and the consequences are as far apart as heaven and earth. So long as awareness is not lost, carrying firewood and hauling water are all practice.
Returning to the Present Moment

, the author writes in this book: “When I was in India, I lived on the second floor of an ashram. During the day I had to go up and down the stairs many times, and each time I would explore the structure of every step I climbed, the working of the knees, and the shifting of weight. This is a fascinating process, and we must hold this kind of interest toward all our activities—insight, exploring how everything happens.”
It must be especially explained that:
1. When aware, one must not only be aware of the object of awareness (the perceived) but also know that one is being aware (the perceiver)—do not sink into the object of awareness.
2. So-called “focus” does not mean staring fixedly at the object of awareness, but rather not letting the attention wander (losing attentiveness) so that deluded thoughts arise.
3. Combining the two points above: when aware, be a relaxed, at-ease, and calm observer, observing your own movements.

Beginners should start by training in the auxiliary practice. This has two advantages: first, through training in the auxiliary practice one comes to understand the essentials of awareness of movements, and then applies them to every movement of daily life. Second, practitioners often ask: what is to be done when deluded thoughts fly about? Now, with the auxiliary practice as this precious sword of authority, if deluded thoughts fly about, one immediately performs the auxiliary practice, and the deluded thoughts cease of themselves. In this way the deluded thoughts that so torment one become a training partner for practice.

This auxiliary practice borrows Mr. Li Fengshan’s “level-swinging exercise.” It is a very good practice: it harmonizes the five viscera and six bowels, invigorates the blood and qi, replenishes oxygen and dispels toxins, and makes the joints of the whole body supple.
The essential point of the practice is: no floating thoughts, and a clear and distinct awareness of every movement, so as to cultivate focused, continuous, and lasting awareness. The method is:

Stand with the feet shoulder-width apart, raise both hands level, palms facing down, at shoulder height, fingers extended, with a smile on the face. Begin by swinging both hands backward, then return to the level position, and thus swing easily and naturally back and forth. The count is: one, two, three, four, five, six. For the first four counts, the count is spoken as the hands move backward. “Five, six” are the squatting down and straightening of the knees (two bounces): on the fifth swing, the hands go backward and one bends the knees slightly in a small squat, saying “five”; then the hands come forward, the knees straighten, and one says “six.” The movements should be gentle and relaxed, forming a natural resonance; there is no need to squat very low. When finishing, the hands slowly come to a stop and return naturally to the sides of the body, the eyes gently close, the breath is made even, the whole body relaxes, and then the eyes slowly open. (Videos of the level-swinging exercise are available online, for example:
Standard Demonstration of the Level-Swinging Exercise (Video)
.) After practicing, slowly drink a cup of warm water; this further helps the circulation of blood and qi and steadies the movement of qi.

The level-swinging exercise is a movement that easily reaches the extremities. The ten fingers connect to the heart, and so it can bring about a thorough return flow, purify the five viscera and six bowels, and let the hundred illnesses adjust themselves. Once a day for thirty minutes brings enormous benefit to body and mind. The first ten minutes can bring about circulation through the whole body, the second ten minutes begin to reach the places in the body that are overtaxed, and the third ten minutes begin to adjust the sites of illness, reaching the state where the soft overcomes the hard.

It must be especially emphasized here: perform the level-swinging exercise at least once a day, thirty minutes each time. The reason for such a rigid rule is that, besides being a cultivation of samādhi in movement and being very effective for cultivating awareness, this hand movement has another very important function: cultivating good psychological qualities and a good psychological state. These movements are not at all difficult; anyone can do them, and anyone can keep them up. Yet the fact is otherwise. Where does the problem lie? The problem lies in our habitual nature: the mind will not quiet down or settle, but is like a wild horse, a cunning ape, a mad elephant. You can try an experiment yourself: while practicing, if the mind becomes fretful, or if you think of other things you have to do, you immediately cannot continue. But if you turn the thought around: practice is like saving your head from fire, it is the foremost matter—can the things you want to do really not wait even thirty minutes? If I cannot even keep up this practice, what practice am I doing! At once the mind becomes cool and steady, and one can practice through to the end. This is where the wonder of “when the mind turns, the circumstances turn” lies. If there really is something so very important that it must be done and thought through at once, then stop, finish it and think it through, and then practice without any lingering concern.

Of course, those with stronger adjustment reactions may reduce the practice time, and after the body returns to normal, gradually restore it to thirty minutes each time. If the body is unsuited to standing and squatting, one may also swing while seated, with the same effect.

The Sūtra of the Secret Essentials of Chan says: “Advance with a single mind, as if saving your head from fire, and do not let the mind be self-indulgent.” For practice, good psychological qualities and a good psychological state are very important; therefore the worthies of old cultivated all kinds of austerities to temper themselves, so as to cultivate good psychological qualities and a good psychological state.

There is another exercise for cultivating good psychological qualities and a good psychological state: each day eat one meal of awareness (being clear and distinct about every movement of eating, without straying into this and that). Admonish yourself: if I cannot even keep up this practice, what practice am I doing! After doing it for a long time, when the mind has become cool and steady, you will feel its wonder.
Mencius said:

“Therefore, when Heaven is about to confer a great charge upon this man, it will surely first make his mind bitter, labor his sinews and bones, starve his body and skin, reduce him to utter poverty, and thwart and confound whatever he does, so as to stir his mind and toughen his nature, and
(increase)
add to what he was not able to do.”

Translation: Therefore, when Heaven is about to confer a great charge upon such a man, it will surely first make his mind bitter and afflicted, labor his sinews and bones, starve his body with hunger and cold, cause him to suffer poverty and peril, confound everything he does, and make him meet with repeated setbacks. By these means it refines and tempers his spirit so that it rises up, makes his character firm, brave, and indomitable, and adds to the abilities he did not originally possess. (For full annotations see
Born in Sorrow and Dying in Ease

In insight meditation, awareness of the rising and falling of the abdomen is often used as the basic training for awareness, with excellent results. On this, the Burmese Venerable Mahāsi gave a masterly instruction:

“With each breath, the abdomen rises and falls. One should begin to attend to this movement, observing the abdomen with the mind. When you breathe in, you will find the abdomen rising; when you breathe out, the abdomen falls. When the abdomen rises, the mind should note ‘rising’; when it falls, the mind should note ‘falling.’ If this movement is not clear, you may place your hand on the abdomen. But do not change the breathing: do not deliberately slow it down or speed it up, and do not breathe too forcefully. If you change the breathing, it will make you feel tired. Breathe naturally, and attend to the rising and falling movement of the abdomen. Note (or label) with the mind, not by repeating aloud.

(Note: there are mainly two ways of breathing: chest breathing and abdominal breathing. Chest breathing depends chiefly on the movement of the ribs and breastbone; when inhaling, the chest expands front to back and side to side. Because the air enters the lungs directly, the chest cavity expands on this account, while the abdomen stays flat. The breathing here is the abdominal breathing of the natural-order method: on inhaling, gently expand the abdominal muscles (the abdomen rises); on exhaling, gently contract the abdominal muscles (the abdomen falls). Compared with chest breathing, this way of breathing has many benefits for bodily health.)

In insight meditation, names and what is said are not important; what truly matters is to know and to be aware. In attending to the rising of the abdomen, one must follow it from the beginning of the movement all the way to the end of the whole rising process, as though seeing it with the eyes. The same is true of attending to the falling movement. When attending to the rising movement, the aware mind must be kept in step with the rising movement; movement and awareness must be synchronized, like dropping a stone that hits the target exactly. The same is true of the falling movement.

When attending to the movement of the abdomen, the mind may wander here and there. At such a time the mind should note: ‘wandering, wandering.’ After noting this once or twice, the wandering mind will stop, and we then return to attending to the rising and falling of the abdomen. If you find that the mind has arrived somewhere, label it ‘arriving, arriving,’ and then return to the movement of the abdomen. If you think of meeting someone, label it ‘meeting, meeting,’ and then return to the rising and falling of the abdomen. If you think of someone and converse with him, label it ‘talking, talking.’

In short, whenever any thought or recollection arises, it must be attended to (or labeled). If you imagine, label it ‘imagining.’ If you think, give it ‘thinking.’ If you plan, give it ‘planning.’ If you perceive, give it ‘perceiving.’ If you recollect, give it ‘recollecting.’ If you feel happy, give it ‘happiness.’ If you feel bored, give it ‘boredom.’ If you feel glad, give it ‘gladness.’ If you feel discouraged, give it ‘discouragement.’ Attending to all these activities of the mind consciousness is called ‘mindfulness of mind.’
When it is attended to, it disappears. Then we return to attending to the rising and falling of the abdomen.” (See
Practical Insight Meditation
[Turning like a crank] A figure for working day and night without stop.

For a practitioner, what one does does not matter; what matters is the state one is in while doing it. If one is in a state of awareness, even a trifling matter is of great significance; if awareness is lost, then however great the matter one does, it is no more than planting the causes of rebirth.

In daily life, whatever one does, one must be aware of every movement: be aware when dressing and eating, be aware when walking and opening doors, be aware when making a phone call, be aware when moving the mouse before the computer,

In order to cultivate awareness quickly, one must keep awareness of movements unbroken throughout the twenty-four hours of the day, and by no means work for one day and freeze for ten. When there is movement, one must be aware; when there is no movement, one performs the auxiliary practice or some small movement of one’s own devising in order to be aware. In fact, some routine chores of daily life, such as dressing, eating, washing the face, brushing the teeth, rising, sitting down, opening doors, and walking, can all be made into practices of awareness of movements, done with keen interest, so as to form the habit of never being separated from awareness. As the saying goes, “The fist never leaves the hand, the song never leaves the mouth.” Our practice must have this same spirit: in every movement, never apart from awareness. As soon as one opens one’s eyes in the morning, remind yourself: today I must maintain awareness, be aware in everything. For example, when drinking water or eating, was every mouthful noticed? When sitting down or rising, was it all noticed? When walking, was every step noticed? First do these few things well, and then unfold it all comprehensively. One must cultivate the habit of awareness of movements; this point is of the utmost importance. In fact, practice is simply cultivating the mind and rectifying one’s conduct, and its key is to overcome karmic hindrances and transform bad habits—for example, transforming the habit of ceaseless deluded thinking into the habit of ceaseless awareness.

Deeply believe that “one reaps in proportion to what one sows”; therefore, in practice, ask only about the sowing and not about the harvest. Once awareness has been cultivated, all problems are solved. Reflect constantly: am I aware? Master, keep awake!
[Awake] Clear in mind and spirit. For a practitioner, falling into deluded thinking or into torpor is to be unclear in mind and spirit, because one has no mastery over oneself.

Awareness must turn like a crank (without pause): throughout the twenty-four hours of the day, be aware of every movement, advancing diligently without slackening. It is said that a fly once came and settled on the Buddha’s face, and the Buddha gently brushed it away with his hand. Then he made the gesture of brushing again. The disciples asked in wonder: “World-Honored One, the first time you waved your hand was to drive away the fly; what was the second wave for?” The Buddha answered: “The first was an unconscious movement, made without awareness; so I made the second movement with awareness, to correct it.” This manifestation by the Buddha was to teach his disciples:
every movement must be clearly and distinctly noticed; a movement made without awareness is ignorance, and one must correct it at once.

In fact, the many devices of the Chan school are only meant to make you block the stream of deluded thoughts beneath the mind-root, and right where it is blocked, look into your original face. To block it by awareness of movements is in truth far less laborious, and no matter whether one’s faculties are sharp or dull, everyone can do it. You should know that awareness of movements without thinking and without thought is precisely the cultivation of samādhi in movement; never slight it as shallow and easy.
In the Great Sūtra of Mindfulness, the Buddha says:

“When a monk is walking, he clearly knows: ‘I am walking.’ When standing, he clearly knows: ‘I am standing.’ When sitting, he clearly knows: ‘I am sitting.’ When lying down, he clearly knows: ‘I am lying down.’ In whatever posture, he clearly knows it. He then observes the body internally, observes the body externally, and observes the body both internally and externally. Thus he observes the phenomena constantly arising in the body, he observes the phenomena constantly ceasing in the body, and he observes both the arising and the ceasing of phenomena in the body. He then clearly knows: ‘This is the body!’ Having cultivated the state in which there is only awareness and only contemplation, he transcends attachment and no longer craves anything in the world of body and mind. Monks! This is how a monk observes the body as body.”
So how does one cultivate awareness and maintain it at all times and in all places? How does one turn daily life into practice and delight in it? The Collected Works of Thich Nhat Hanh says:

Perhaps you will ask: when washing dishes, binding books (binding books was Thich Nhat Hanh’s daily work, and in the book he tells how he turned this work into practice), or working in a factory or office, how exactly does one cultivate awareness? I think you must seek the answer for yourself. So long as you do your utmost to keep the inner light of awareness bright, you will in the end find the way that suits you.”

For a Chan master, when washing dishes the sacred and the mundane can exist together and blend without conflict. To be aware, while washing dishes, of the process of the hands touching the dishes and the water is an experience full of the sacred and the marvelous; but the key point still lies in washing with continuity and with attention to the present moment.”

There are many other things to do in life: tending the garden, cooking and washing clothes, cleaning bowls and chopsticks, binding books, writing. Perhaps these things are not as interesting as drinking tea or walking on a hillside, but if you do them with complete awareness, you will find them quite delightful too. Even washing the bowls and chopsticks after a full meal is a joyful pleasure; every bowl we wash is a miracle.”

Every thought and every movement within awareness is sacred. In this luminous realm the boundary between the sacred and the mundane has been erased. I admit that I take longer than others to wash the dishes, but I live in the present moment at every moment, and my mind is truly happy. Washing dishes is both means and end—in other words, washing dishes is not only for the sake of clean dishes, but also for the sake of washing dishes, so that one stays aware at every moment of washing them. If I cannot wash the dishes with a joyful mind and only want to finish as quickly as possible so that I can go drink tea, then I will be equally unable to enjoy that cup of tea to the full. Though the cup of tea is in my hand, my mind is still dwelling on other things; thus the flavor of the tea and the pleasure of tasting it all vanish, and my mind is forever suspended in the ‘future’ and can never live in the ‘present’
Remember: what you do does not matter; what matters is that you are focused and aware in what you do.
Q: Keeping awareness of movements turning like a crank is easy to speak of, but very difficult to put into practice. What is to be done?

A: This is not strange, for since beginningless kalpas one has formed the habit of ceaseless deluded thinking—habit has become nature, has become instinct—whereas awareness of movements is brand new. To transform a deeply rooted bad habit (deluded thinking) into a brand new good habit (awareness of movements), one must expend great effort and undergo great training.

There is a story: a woman urged her husband to recite the Buddha’s name, but the husband was slack and lazy by nature, and could never do it. Fearing that he would fall into hell to suffer in the future, the wife said to her husband: “I will hang a small bell on the door. When you go in and out, as soon as you hear the bell, recite the Buddha’s name at once, and it will keep you safe.” The husband answered: “What difficulty is there in that? I will do as you say.” Thereafter, each time he went in or out and heard the doorbell ring, he recited the Buddha’s name a few times. He thought the method quite good, for it saved his wife from constantly urging him. Time flew like an arrow, and the days and months like a shuttle; the husband, entering old age, fell ill and could not rise, and soon died of his illness. After death he did indeed fall into hell. Because his evil karma in the world was heavy, he did not believe in good dharmas and did not do good deeds; so the ghost attendants threw him into an iron cauldron to be boiled. It happened that when a ghost attendant jabbed him with a trident, the copper bells on the trident rang, and the husband, thinking it was the doorbell, recited the Buddha’s name aloud again and again, and so was delivered.

This story tells us that it is much easier to use skillful methods and rules to help form good habits. Now, to form the good habit of awareness of movements, you may set yourself rules: first, be aware of the movement when rising and when sitting down; second, when walking (including walking indoors), be aware of every step; third, when eating, be aware of every bite and chew. Before going to sleep at night, review how you did today. Grade yourself on five levels—very good (5 points), good (4), fair (3), poor (2), very poor (1)—and record it in a notebook. Every Sunday evening, make a small summary of the seven days of that week, calculate the average score, assess how the week went and how the next week should be improved and raised, and write it all in detail in the notebook. On this basis, make a monthly summary and a yearly summary. This notebook may be named the Record of Self-Knowledge. That people fall rather than rise is owing to the suffering of being unable to know themselves. Now, with the Record of Self-Knowledge, examining oneself day by day, week by week, month by month, year by year, if one carries it out earnestly, there is no fear of failing. The Great Emperor of Mount Tai instructs:
“To do good
(blessing)
is like the grass of a spring garden: no one sees it grow, yet it increases daily; to do evil
(blessing)
is like a whetstone: no one sees it wear, yet it diminishes daily. Calamity and blessing shift in secret
(calamity and blessing shift in the dark)
, and the deluded are unaware
(the deluded cannot perceive it)
For study and practice today, it may be written as:
awareness,
(prajñā)
is like the grass of a spring garden: no one sees it grow, yet it increases daily; deluded thinking,
(prajñā)
is like a whetstone: no one sees it wear, yet it diminishes daily. Birth and death shift in secret
(birth and death shift in the dark)
, and the deluded are unaware
(the deluded cannot perceive it)

Hereafter, when cultivating awareness of sensations, awareness of breathing, awareness of the present moment, awareness of mental states, and Chan contemplation, use the Record of Self-Knowledge throughout, and you will surely succeed.

Drawing on the worthies of old, here is another example: Mr. Zhao Kangjing of the Song dynasty used a bottle and black and white beans for the work of the mind-ground: when a good thought arose, he dropped in a white bean; when an evil thought arose, he dropped in a black bean. At first the beans in the bottle were more black than white, but later white gradually came to outnumber black. In the course of time, they were pure white with no black. Going further, he reached the state where mind and objects were both forgotten and he entered the state of no deliberation; and so even the bottle and the beans were abandoned and no longer used.
Q: To remind myself to be aware at all times and in all places, I am always silently repeating “aware”—may I do that?
A: You may. This is a very skillful method.
The work of awareness of movements generally passes through the following stages:

1. At the beginning, deluded thoughts still arise alongside awareness of movements. This is because the power of awareness is weak; so long as one persists in the auxiliary practice, it will soon improve.

2. When one is focused in awareness of movements, there are no deluded thoughts; but as soon as one relaxes a little, deluded thoughts arise. It takes considerable effort to return to the state in which “awareness of movements means no deluded thoughts.”

3. When aware of movements, there are no deluded thoughts; but once one forgets awareness, one falls into deluded thinking without knowing it. Only after a while does one discover that one is daydreaming. Yet as soon as one returns to awareness of movements, the deluded thoughts cease of themselves.

4. When aware of movements, there are no deluded thoughts; but once one forgets awareness, one falls into deluded thinking. Still, one is already able to discover the daydreaming relatively quickly. As soon as one returns to awareness of movements, the deluded thoughts cease of themselves.
5. When aware of movements, there are no deluded thoughts; but if one is the least bit careless, deluded thoughts slip in through the gap—though one is able to discover them in good time.
6. The practice becomes one continuous piece, and deluded thoughts find no gap to enter.
